speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: NEGOTIATIONS FOR CONTRACT WITH THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce in a position to give a report to the house with regard to the wheat negotiations between the government of the United Kingdom and the government of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: NEGOTIATIONS FOR CONTRACT WITH THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I rather expected that I would be asked such a question to-day, and I came prepared to make a brief statement to the house with regard to the progress being made in negotiations looking towards a wheat contract between Canada and the United Kingdom.
For the past ten days negotiations have been carried on between experts representing this country and the United Kingdom. Substantial progress has been made in regard to the terms of such an agreement, in spite of the difficulties involved in placing the sale of a large volume of wheat on a contract basis for an extended period. A number of important considerations have now arisen which must become a matter of reference to the Canadian government and the United Kingdom government. As soon as these matters have been dealt with by the respective governments, negotiations will be resumed on the terms of the proposed contract.

In my humble view the revenue and the increase of the debt during war time, the increase of the debt through borrowing on the one hand, and on the other hand the non-war and war expenditures during that period, should balance. As a foreword may I say that the country spends the revenue which comes from taxes, and when there is not enough revenue to meet the expenditures, then there is some borrowing. During the war the borrowing was done through victory loans. The money which has been received from taxation and from victory loans should balance with the non-war and the war expenditures of the same period. This statement seems clear, and everyone may agree with it in principle.
According to the figures given by the Department of Finance on May 27, 1946, at page 1881 of Hansard, the total revenue from September 1, 1930, to February 28, 1946, was $12,681 million. The debt at March 31, 1945, which is the latest figure I have, was $15,712 million. This amount of $7,558 million which has not been accounted for represents $2,000 million more than all the deposits in the ten Canadian chartered banks. It is one-fourth the total expenditure of $30,000 million during the war. It is a very serious matter.
I was the only member to complain against the Bank of Canada when it was established. Now the books of the Bank of Canada apparently balance, but there is a secret; there is a mystery behind the doors of the Bank of Canada, and it is impossible to get any information about that. When the banking committee studied the Bank of Canada Act a couple of years ago the attention of hon. members was ably directed elsewhere by a discussion of the supposed hidden reserves of the banks. Much noise was made about it, but no member of parliament took advantage of that unique opportunity to get information about the Bank of Canada itself. I warned some members that a trick was being played; I warned the house and country that it was dangerous to have amounts unaccounted for when we debated the gift made in 1943. But that was a trivial matter; it was a casual matter of no importance!
Now there is an amount of $7,500 million which apparently is unaccounted for. In May I asked for information about the amount of the debt to the end of the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946. The only information I got was to the end of the fiscal year preceding. Every business man has accounts showing the operation of his business each morning when he comes to his office. He finds that information on his desk each day. I wonder if the Minister of Finance is not informed day after day as to the amounts of the debt of Canada. If we are to be the bankers of the world, then business should be done otherwise, because that figure of $7,500 million represents the amounts collected in several of the victory loan campaigns.
I do not cast any doubt upon the honesty and integrity of the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary assistant. I do not cast any aspersions of dishonesty on anyone in the Bank of Canada. But the day of mystery should be ended. The time has come when the House of Commons should scrutinize the business of the Bank of Canada; and the Minister of Finance should be responsible to the people, just as in the days of Fielding, White and Jim Robb.
Parliament is in the impossible position of being unable to get information about the business of the country. Money is spread everywhere, but when we ask for an accounting it is hard to get. Probably it will be made later. I wonder if that is the reason 63260-177J
the budget has been delayed so long. Perhaps it may be made. As this document states:
This excess would be reflected in the books of the government by increases under various accounts classified as active assets (cash, loans, investments, etc.)
When Mr. Dunning was Minister of Finance I asked him for information about the personnel of the Bank of Canada. But his reply was, "No, that is a secret". When Mr. Bennett, upon my advice to one of his secretaries, left for the Antipodes, he took with him a doorman from the Bank of Canada named Brooks. Upon his return I asked the government of that day if Brooks' salary had been paid by Mr. Bennett or by the Bank of Canada while he was travelling with Mr. Bennett. The answers by the Prime Minister and by Mr. Bennett were that I had been very bold in asking such a question, and that no member of parliament should inquire about the Bank of Canada. They said' it was very bad manners to ask if Brooks had been paid by the Bank of Canada or by R. B. Bennett.
We are responsible to the people of Canada for the money that is spent outside and inside the country. We must be in a position to inform our constituents when they ask us for information in these matters. It is our duty; are we neglectful of it?
We live in strange times. On one occasion I complained about a man who, it was supposed, had sold the same coal three times; but no one was scandalized. Everyone considered him smart. These are the signs of the times. We are neglectful; we are careless; we pay no attention to these matters. Then, afterwards, some people will complain about taxation. They are ready to throw away their money outside, anywhere. We help the world, but we cannot look after our own business.
Sir, you will remember how many times I have insisted that the Minister of Finance bring in some reform in the matter of public accounts. The help I got was from two hon. members opposite, the hon. member for Broadview, and the hon. member for Davenport, who is now in his seat. Now when members of parliament complain about high taxation, they will remember that they made no move to reform public accounts. They voted for the loans which we had not the means to make. Having done that, they cannot complain about high taxation; it would seem that they want it. They are responsible before the people of Canada for that high taxation. I wonder if they will not realize the time has come to make a check

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
on public business, to scrutinize the operations of the Bank of Canada and to make the Minister of Finance responsible again to the House of Commons in conformity with the old principle of ministerial responsibility.
I have asked information about government agencies, the chief of which is the Bank of Canada, including its subsidiaries, such as the foreign exchange control board. That board, it will be recalled, is operated by a man trained by Montagu Norman, and another man, who were doing so much at the Bank of International Settlements in Switzerland, and who during the war were shaking hands with Germans under the table. Those people are here. They are supposed to be internationally minded; I am not. I am nationally minded, although I am not a nationalist. I consider that the Canadians who are here should be considered first, and before any other peoples in the world. It is in their defence I speak to-day. As usual, perhaps I shall have the support of one member-or two. If there are two, there will be a crowd in support of my contentions.
I wonder what the people of Canada think about it. These figures are available; they can be collected by the Bank of Canada. It is very easy; anyone could do it. It is only a matter of bringing together the various increases under different accounts classified as active assets, cash loans and investments. Let it be done; let us place responsibility where it should be. Let us say that it has gone somewhere-to the Atlantic, the Pacific, the north pole, or the south pole; we do not know where. But the money has gone.
Let us suppose that one has an estate of 1100,000, and that it is to be administered by someone who, while honest, may be incompetent. When the time comes for the rendition of accounts, they are rendered for only $75,000. Where has the other quarter gone? Where is the $25,000? No one knows. It is unaccounted for. That is the situation here.
I have simply given in miniature the true picture, which I believe to be my duty. I have informed the house. I wonder if the budget debate will simply be a matter of patting on the back, saying that everyone has done wonderful work, and that we must not disturb those gentlemen in the Bank of Canada who are so very competent and who are under such heavy strain because they work so hard!
One time I asked Mr. Dunning how much Graham Towers received. When I asked if it was $35,000 the minister was indignant, and replied, "Not at all; it is only $30,000." In spite of all this incompetence, which has scandalized me, I see a further notice in the

papers that these fellows in the Department of Finance are to have a boost in salary because. they have done so magnificently. Yet they cannot render accounts for $7,500 million out of expenditures of $30,000 million.
A salary of $30,000 is a more pittance.

It is a small thing. I
hope I have awakened the. house to its responsibilities, and I hope that every hon. member, no matter to what party he belongs, realizes that he has a responsibility to protect the Canadian people against the incompetency of men who perhaps wdth the best motives in the world have ruled rich concerns in the state.
Then a word about university degrees. Oh, that is a bad thing. I remember that one of these men came to Mr. Bennett and said, "Mr. Bennett, you are not acknowledged as you should be on the North American continent. You should be made a doctor of laws in all the universities of this country." Mr. Bennett said, "Well, you are fair to me; you are a decent chap, and I appreciate what you say." Then Mr. Bennett was made doctor of laws in universities where he had never placed his foot. This is just a form of flattery. These people wear their mortarboards and they begin to think that they are held in higher esteem by the Canadian people. It is still done, and perhaps it is something that should be done more generously.
Members of parliament show a lack of courage and are unfaithful to their duty when they do not denounce those who consider themselves to be high above us and who really govern this country. If I had the proper words at my command I would tell the Minister of Finance and his assistant that I am sorry that they have not the nerve to follow what was done for this country by the pioneers and builders of the past, by men like Fielding, White and Robb. Those men were ready to defend the rights of the people within the precincts of parliament, and that is where it should be done.
At first the Bank of Canada was a private concern with individuals subscribing to some of the capital stock. Then it was taken over by the government and became a public institution. I do not know why the Bank of Canada is not abolished. I do not know why the foreign exchange control board is not abolished. I do not know why ministerial responsibility is not exercised again by the Minister of Finance, why there is not responsibility to the members of parliament who in turn are responsible to the people of Canada.

I have said this many times and I am repeating it to-day. It is pretty hard to follow figures when they are being read, but hon. members can read them to-morrow in Hansard. They will then see that there is something behind them. When I am not satisfied with an answer that is given to me I check the figures, and I felt that the discrepancy in the figures that have been given to me was so great that the matter should be brought to the notice of my colleagues in the house, which I have done.

Mr. Chairman, we in the opposition agree with the hon. member for Temiscouata when he says that parliament should have the fullest information and be able to make the strictest examination of the country's accounts. May I add that we are happy to know that the hon. member has disavowed his vow of silence and is once more giving us the benefit of his wisdom.
There is a matter I should like to bring up which has to do with the wartime prices and trade board. For some time the press has reported various small rackets in coupon distribution in different parts of the *. ountry. Ouly to-day La Banque Provinciate du Canada were notified by the wartime prices and trade board that, after July 31 next they will not be permitted to participate in the arrangement for ration coupon banking. The announcement was in the form of a release made outside of parliament while parliament is sitting. The officials of the board explain that this bank has been warned of its method of handling coupon accounts. They say that safeguards recommended by the board to protect the public have not been lived up to by this bank; therefore in the public interest, the board has no alternative but to terminate the arrangements with them. This is the first opportunity we have had in the house to ask what irregularities have been ascertained-because they must have been widespread-how long they have been going oh, and what safeguards recommended by the board were not lived up to. Recently the press reported the investigation had indicated that about a million fake or false butter coupons had found their way into the chartered banks. Apparently the bank in question was warned that its activities were illegal. What measures are being taken to ensure that in common with ordinary wrongdoers they will be prosecuted according to law? I am sure the government would wish to acquaint, the country at the earliest possible opportunity with all the circumstances of this investigation and to indicate what action the government intends to take in order to prevent a repetition of any such practice. If the situation was sufficiently serious to warrant cancellation of the- right of a bank to operate ration coupon banking for the wartime prices and trade board, why is the right not cancelled immediately instead of being continued for over a month?

Mr. Chairman, this is a resolution to vote interim supply of one-twelfth, amounting to 8136,000,000. Fifty years ago last Sunday, on June 23, 1896, the Liberal administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power pledged to retrenchment. The whole year's budget of the first year they were in power amounted to $36,000,000, which is S102.000,000 less than the one-twelfth that is being asked for now. We are spending billions to-day compared with millions then. There are many good business men in this house, but certainly this house does not conduct its business in a businesslike way. We are now being asked to vote one-twelfth of the whole year's supply from March 31, 1946, when hardly any estimates have been passed at all. In a few weeks another one-twelfth will be asked for, and on the 12th of July, no doubt, another one-twelfth. What we are really doing is making post mortem examinations of expenditures. We might just as well go home. John Hampden stood for an important principle wThen he refused ship money to the king. The hon. member for Temiscouata made a good stand last session and the session before; he was contending for a principle, and that is what we should do in this house. We should see that there is a proper examination of the estimates before they are voted.
The House of Commons has gone down in public estimation. The press came into being because of a lack of real parliamentary representation, and the press to-day represents public opinion more than do the members of the House of Commons, because our rights and privileges are continually being taken away from us, with the result that we have this way of doing business. I contend it is all wrong. The principle is entirely wrong. This is the sixty-seventh day of the session, and the budget has not yet been brought down. We shall be considering it in July and the session will go on until August, and probably September before we get through. That will mean that for six months of the year the money will have been spent, voted one-twelfth at a time, but, with very few estimates having been passed, and some of the departments have not yet been called in supply. There was some reason for proceeding in this
2S04

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
way during the war, but the war has been over for a year, and no budget has been brought down yet.
They do things differently at Washington. There they have applied the axe to expenditures. We are a country of only eleven millions of people, with nine provincial governments and all the municipal governments. Over-government and over-taxation is the curse of this country. Expenditures are being made without public control. We used to have an auditor general. He used to have certain powers, but they have been taken away. He is picking up quite a bit after the criticism of his reports and is doing a bit of checking, but it does not amount to anything because there is an official over him called the comptroller of the treasury. You have a war appropriation bill, A, B, C, D, E, and once the accounts go through within the terms of the appropriation bill, the account is stamped and paid over the head of parliament without any control at all. The country will face bankruptcy if we continue to conduct business in that way. A number of small business men have already been driven out of business by the controllers that have been appointed. Only the other day the owner of a house in Toronto was evicted from his own home and taken to Pape Avenue police station in my constituency. Under an absurd housing regulation issued by the housing controller this man could not get into his own home. I have examined these various controllers and boards and it is time they were all wound up.
Take an institution like the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It collects a licence fee of $2.50 and spends public money on capital accounts and yet it is contended that it is a private corporation, not a public corporation. Is it any wonder that the tax rate is as high as it is, and that people cannot pay their income tax? Is it any wonder that the small business man cannot continue in business? There has to be a change for the benefit of the people. Under the comptroller of the treasury we mostly have no control at all of expenditures and no control of the chiselers. There were some real Liberals in 1896. Alexander Mackenzie, it used to be said, slept on the strong-box. He has no counterpart in liberalism to-day. They have even moved his monument into the back yard. Every Tom, Dick and Harry who wants to come to Ottawa and raid the treasury finds no one guarding the nation's strong-box. The people are looking to parliament to do something, and we are doing nothing. If the municipal governments conducted their business the way we conduct ours in this House of Commons, they would be prosecuted under the Municipal 
Act for not having done their duty and would be dismissed at the next municipal election. We have no check on our business or on our expenditure. I do not suppose there is much use in protesting, but this is the place where the protests should be made. We cannot go on indefinitely in this way under this new 1946 type of liberalism, where we are spending money like water over the head of parliament, over the heads of the responsible ministers and without any public check at all. If this is the way we are going to conduct our business it is no wonder that parliamentary institutions are going down and down and down in public estimation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for Temiscouata evidently believes that it is better to give than to receive, because he left the chamber after making his remarks. The only criticism I have to make is of his statement that the information was hard to obtain. He was hasty in making that statement. I do not think he had any right to make it. When he asked for information from the department it was immediately supplied to him, and the suggestion was made that if he could not then reconcile the figures given to him, we would have someone from the department visit him and try to show him exactly what was meant by the statement. As to the rest of his statement, it will be brought to the attention of the minister and of the governor of the bank.
As to the statement made by the hon. member for Lake Centre, I am not familiar with the- matter, but it will also be given attention, and as soon as the information can be obtained it will be brought down. I exipeet that in a very short time there will he an opportunity to discuss this if it is necessary. The estimates for the mounted police will come on just as soon as the estimates for health and welfare have been dealt with, and any information we have can be given at that time. I hope that will meet the hon. member's request.

I would not wish to put the parliamentary secretary in an embarrassing position. But there was a press release on this matter to-day, and I cannot see why parliament should have to wait three or four or five weeks for the estimates of the wartime prices and trade board in order to get the information. I ask the parliamentary assistant to have the information furnished to-day. Parliament is entitled to any information given in press releases and more. I do not want to be unfair to the parliamentary assistant, but I do insist on the information being given now, to-day, before this resolution is passed; otherwise it is just one more instance of parliament

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
being ignored. The hon. member indicated that if it was necessary to give any information, possibly it could be given later. I am sure what he meant was that after the matter had been checked with the wartime prices and trade board the information would be forthcoming. I ask for it to-day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Lake Centre misunderstood what I said.
I said the information would be supplied to him just as soon as possible, possibly when the estimates for the mounted police are brought down, which will be immediately following the National Health and Welfare estimates, probably later to-day, certainly not later than to-morrow. The matter can then be gone into in detail and we can furnish him with all the information in connection with it-not on the estimates of the wartime prices and trade board.

No one knows
whether the matter has been brought to the attention of the Department of Justice. All we know is that the wartime prices and trade board did certain things. The wartime prices and trade board is under the Minister of Finance, who has introduced the resolution now before us. If we wait until later in the afternoon the Minister of Justice may say; of course the matter has never been brought to my attention; you had better get in touch with Finance; and we shall be back again on the regular old performance. We are entitled to the information now. The press release issued to-day says that certain wrongs have been ascertained on the part of La Banque Provinciale du Canada, that apparently it has been neglectful of its duties and responsibilities, to such an extent that, after warning, the board has found it necessary to cancel this bank's right to handle the distribution, allocation, or cashing of coupons. If the matter is as serious as that, surely parliament is entitled to have the information when we are being asked to vote interim supply, part of which will certainly be used for the commodity prices stabilization fund and other activities of the wartime prices and trade board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not disagree at all with what the hon. member has to say. I think he is entitled to the information, and I promise to get it to him as soon as I possibly can. subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of bill No. 138, to amend the Railway Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Trains moving in reverse.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: May I endeavour to persuade the minister to make a statement?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
The amendment sought in this bill is simple, and I think will commend itself to the house. It has to do with the movement of a locomotive and its tender operating in reverse. It happens from time to time that locomotives must move in reverse, and the section has always aimed at protecting the public when the locomotive is moving over unprotected crossings, by posting a man on the front of the tender. This amendment seeks to eliminate the placing of that man on the tender.
Perhaps I should give a brief history of the legislation having to do with this section.
The origin of section 310 was section 276 of the Railway Act, which was passed in 1901. The language of that section was very clear. It stipulated that in any city, town or village, on any train passing over or along a highway at rail level not headed by an engine moving forward in the ordinary manner, the company should station on that part of the train or of the tender, if that is in front, a person who should warn persons standing on or crossing or about to cross the track of such railway. The railway brotherhoods objected strenuously to the posting of that man. They did so for many reasons, one of them being that when the locomotive completed its run the engineman often was required to leave the engine, after being in a very wTarm temperature for hours, and come down on the tender in

Railway Act

order to ride the tender back to the roundhouse. Over the years they objected strenuously to that. The various railway companies admitted that there was some foundation for the objections raised by the brotherhood and attempted to rectify the difficulty by having an amendment passed in 1910, which was chapter 50 of the statutes of Canada for that year. But that amendment gave a discretion to the board of railway commissioners, and that did not work out satisfactorily. It was not until 1917 that satisfaction apparently was obtained by eliminating the words, "or of the tender if that is in front" so that by chapter 37 of the statutes of 1917 it apparently became no longer necessary for a man to be posted on a tender when a train was moving backward. Perhaps here I should just read that section, because it is pertinent. Section 276 as enacted by chapter 37 of 1917 reads as follows:
Whenever in any city, town or village, any train not headed by an engine is passing over or along a highway at rail level which is not adequately protected by gates or otherwise, the company shall station on that part of the train, which is then foremost, a person who shall warn persons standing on, or crossing, or about to cross the track of such railway.
The words "or of the tender, if that is in the front" were eliminated, so that it became no longer necessary to post a man on the tender. But following an accident which took place in the city of Hull the privy council placed an interpretation on this section which decided that a locomotive and a tender is a train, So by virtue of this interpretation it became necessary again to place a man on the tender. I say this because the intention of parliament in 1917 was quite clear. It was the intention then to do away with the posting of that man, but parliament's intention was interpreted in a different way by the privy council.
In order to meet the intention of parliament as enacted in 1917; in order to meet the wishes of the brotherhoods, of the railway association of Canada, this amendment is now sought; and it is framed in such a way that the words "or its tender" have now been added after the word "engine", the effect of this being that the legal interpretation of the word "engine" is now overcome, so that in the opinion of the law officers of the Department of Transport it will become no longer necessary to post a man on the front of a tender when the locomotive and its tender are moving in reverse.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
What is the position if the locomotive and tender are shunting a train of three cars behind them? Does the man go on the end car?
[Mr. Chevrier.l

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Yes. It is necessary for a man to be posted on the end of a number of cars if they are being pushed backwards by a locomotive and its tender. I said a moment ago that this legislation was requested by the joint legislative committee of the railway transportation brotherhoods. It has been endorsed by the railway association of Canada and approved by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. I should like to read an opinion of Sir Henry Drayton in which he covers the point fully. This was an opinion he gave prior to the enactment of the statute of 1917, when he said:
In the opinion of the operating department-
That is of the board of railway commissioners.
-a man on the tender when the engine leads the movement, although backing, serves no useful purpose. In the ease of almost every engine, as a matter of fact, the engineer has at least as good if not a better view of the track in front of him as in the case of a front movement, a tender nearly always being shorter than the boiler and other engine works in front of the cab; and, in the case of a reverse movement, as a usual thing, there is no possibility of the view being obscured either by smoke or steam.
In other words, it would appear that, if a man on the tender is necessary, a man is also necessary in the front of every locomotive operating over crossings.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: What has become of the objection raised by the railway brotherhoods, that they did not desire their members to get out on the back in cold weather?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: This meets the objection. This amendment to the Railway Act is being enacted to meet their objection.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: How does it meet it?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: By doing away with the necessity of posting a man on the tender of the train moving in reverse. That is what the amendment does.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: What protection is the public given in this regard?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: The public does not need protection in this matter. The opinion given by Sir Henry Drayton, and that of the board of transport commissioners, is that locomotives are so long to-day that the engine man or the fireman who is in the cab of a locomotive has a much better view of objects crossing the highway than would a man posted down below at the foot of the tender.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: That is probably correct.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
WThat happens when a train is backing up, with the engine and tender probably a quarter of a mile away? Does the brakeman not have to be on the end of the car going forward?

Railway Act

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: Yes; it is necessary to post a man on the rear of the train. The law remains the same in that respect as it was before. This has to do only with the tender, not with trains which might be in the front of the tender.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: In the circumstances set out in the act, the engine and tender if backing up would really be at the wrong end of the train.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: The engineer might be able to see just as well; however it was always my understanding that the forward brakeman was the one who stood on the front of the tender when it was backing up. I did not think the engineer or fireman did that.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: That is what brought about the discussion in the matter. When the act was passed in 1917 the brakeman did not do it. Either the fireman or the engine man had to go down from the cab, and go out in front. Because of the protests of the brotherhoods, for a time the companies used yardmen who were doing work at the stations. They would jump on the front end of the tender. There was difficulty about that, and finally the decision was made to amend the section by doing away with the man altogether. It was not done by the brakeman.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: It was done by the forward brakeman.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: No, by the engine man or fireman.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: It was done by the brake-man on the train, but not on the tender.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: It is my memory that the forward brakeman, who frequently rides in the engine, would get down and go to what would then be the front of the train, and warn' the people to stand back. I am afraid if we eliminate the necessity of someone being on the so-called front of the train when it is backing up, with the long engines and long tenders now in use-some of the cylindrical water tanks are mammoth in size- the public will not have all the necessary protection required. Is the minister satisfied that there will be ample protection?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Yes, and for more than one reason. In connection with an amendment of this nature it is customary to submit the suggestion to the board of transport commissioners. They have an operating branch which goes into these matters thoroughly, and I am informed they have approved this amendment. As far back at 1942, as a result 63260-1781
of the demands of all parties concerned-the men and the railway association-an order in council was passed under the War Measures Act doing this very thing. It has been in effect now for at least three years.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: They are compelled to give ample warning with whistles and bells.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: Is there any limit to the speed at which a train is allowed to back up?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: Yes, there is a limit under the Railway Act. I do not know what it is, offhand, but I can find out.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I hope every consideration will be given by the board of transport commissioners and by the government to the elimination of level crossings. I have been a passenger on two trains which hit automobiles, and have seen something of the destruction caused. In one instance a priest and his driver were killed, and in the other a family were pitched out and had to be taken to the hospital. I do not know what happened to them' afterwards. We have too many level crossings in Canada, particularly along the main lines of the railways. No matter how much protection we may give in circumstances such as are envisaged in the bill, we do not get to the root of the problem of level crossings. Most countries have endeavoured to get- rid of them. During the period of unemployment before the war we were told that one of the projects which would receive consideration by the government elected in 1935 was the elimination of level crossings. I know of only two or three which were eliminated. Far too many of them are still in existence, for the safety of the public. These are different from the days when we had horses and buggies. Traffic moves quickly along the highways, and I take this opportunity to urge upon the government the necessity of making plans to eliminate as soon as possible the level crossing menace. I have in mind highways very close to Regina, where one drives down beside the railway and then makes a sudden turn to cross. One night while driving I saw what I thought was an automobile coming in the opposite direction. It turned out to be a train, and it was only by accelerating very quickly that I managed to get across. The train happened to be a flier, although I had thought it was an automobile on the other side of the track. I just managed to get across; otherwise I would not have been here to-day- and some people might have been thankful for it.
Railway Act

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Who is asking for this legislation, anyway? Last Thursday evening I made reference to the large number of people who are killed on level crossings. A man should be on the engine tender, and I see no reason for making the change. Surely there is such a thing as public rights and safety. The people have just as much right on the highways as the railway companies, especially when the highways were built before the railways came along.
An application has been made before the board of transport commissioners for the building of a subway to eliminate the danger at the Jones avenue and Woodbine avenue crossings in the constituency I represent. That subway should be built, because there is ten times the amount of traffic at that point that there is farther down the line where there is a subway at Victoria park avenue. There is enough loss of life as it is without adding any further to the number of accidents that will happen if this amendment to relieve the railway companies of responsibility is passed. At present they are under the obligation to station a man to warn persons that an engine is moving. There is considerable traffic along the waterfront in Toronto and there is always danger in the moving of coal and other cars. The same thing applies to other parts of the city. Surely some consideration should be given to the public in an effort to prevent the terrible loss of life that occurs at level crossings. Only last week-end twenty-nine people were killed in eastern Canada from various causes, and it is horrible to see the way human life is being sacrificed at level crossings without considering the economic wastage, loss of employment and earnings which run into hundreds of millions. All this is quite apart from the human suffering that occurs.
This bill ought to go to the railway committee in order that the public may be protected. What is the use of having a committee when they never or seldom meet?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: They are meeting now.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I am not opposed to the railways because I believe they have certain rights and they do a great deal of good. In congested cities and towns and in many of the villages along the Lake Shore road there are many danger spots and we should not be relieving the railway companies of providing reasonable and proper methods of protection. In Toronto millions and millions of dollars were spent to build the viaduct. The waterfront roads were there long before the railways came, but the city paid one-third of the cost, something which they had no right to

do, in order to provide the necessary protection. The cost to the taxpayers was between S13,000.000 and $14,000,000.
What has become of the policy of the government in connection with level crossings? A return was brought down this session showing that hardly any money is being spent on grade crossings. They used to spend from two to three millions a year on grade separation account, but this was permitted to become a dead letter during the war. This bill ought to go to the railway committee in order that a report may be made and municipalities and others who are aggrieved heard. They have had no notice of this bill. It may have been advertised in the Canada Gazette, but we should go slow in a matter like this when human life is involved. We are far behind Great Britain and the United States in connection with grade separation and the protection of the public. The time is coming when the public will stand for this no longer because so many of them are being killed.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
I do not disagree with the matter because I believe he has given quite a lot of consideration to this matter, but I am a little reluctant to vote for a thing like this. I am not going to speak as a parliamentarian; I am going to speak as one who has built locomotives. A locomotive is built to go forward; it is streamlined for that purpose and the engineer can see only ahead with ease. It was expected that when the locomotive had to reverse there would be a lookout on the tender to guide the engineer.
The minister says that the brotherhoods have appealed for this. I know from my locomotive experience that there have been many men killed or maimed for life when a proper lookout was not maintained when the locomotive was just going to the roundhouse. As I understand the bill, when a train is reversing there will be the usual lookout, but this amendment applies only to an engine and tender.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: An engine and a tender is a train.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: But when there is a train attached there will be a proper lookout?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: I think this is a mistake in the interests of safety.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: The railway brotherhoods do not think so.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
That may be so, but I would put the safety of the people before what the brotherhoods want. A lot of men have had to be out in the cold in order to protect the safety of this nation.

Transport Stores

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peterborough West asked about the speed of trains moving in reverse. It is ten miles an hour across highways.
With reference to what was said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Broadview, I would point out that I made a lengthy statement on the elimination of level crossings on the second reading of another bill to amend the Railway Act which was brought down by the hon. member for York West. At that time I dealt with the question of safety at these crossings.
I pointed out that a committee composed of certain members of the board of transport commissioners had been set up to go across this country to study grade crossings deemed to be dangerous, in order that they might be eliminated as a post-war project. That work is being done. While a report has not been made, the investigation is being carried on.
It has been said that no notice of this bill was given. It has been the law now for three years and there have been no accidents. It seems to have met with the general approval of all persons concerned.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: You are just defining the word "engine"?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Yes. With reference to the point raised that this might take away certain rights from the public, I would point out that it is the other way around if anything. The danger is to the man on the tender. Experience has shown that it is the man on the tender who finds himself in the more difficult position. He is there without any protection. Should a train moving in reverse strike a motorcar, he is more likely to be injured than the man at the wheel of the motorcar. I am not saying that there is no danger to the man in the motorcar, but that is the case.
I want to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that this whole matter was thoroughly debated in 1917 and the house took from the then section 276 the words, "or of the tender if that is in front," because parliament then thought that the elimination of those words were necessary. Had it not been for the decision of the privy council which held otherwise in the case in 1922 to which I referred, there would be no necessity for this amendment. It is just to circumvent and do away with the interpretation by the privy council of section 310 as it stood that this amendment is thought necessary.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Perhaps I did not get my point across to the minister. When an engineer wants to move his engine in reverse
he must put his head out in order to look back. He cannot sit in the position in which he usually sits to drive the engine and look back at the same time.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: The engineer has a tremendous responsibility if he is to be the lookout man when approaching a level crossing. I would remind the minister that both engines and tenders of to-day are much greater in length than they were fifteen or twenty years ago. Even in that short period there has been a great change in the construction of locomotives and tenders. There is increased danger of course in storms, fog and night driving when the view is obstructed to some extent. Does this relieve the railway of any responsibility for accidents at level crossings under those conditions?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: The railway is relieved of the necessity of posting a man on the tender, but it is not relieved of legal liability if negligence can be shown. The common law right and the statute right still remain.

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext: The minister is of the opinion that the public is as fully protected without the man being posted there?

subtopic: TRAINS OR CARS MOVING IN REVERSE OVER HIGHWAY CROSSINGS

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of bill 139, to amend the Department of Transport Stores Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Inventory.
Transport Stores
Mr. MaoNICOL: Would the minister give an explanation of the amendment? Just what are the advantages and the reasons for increasing the inventory from $1,250,000?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext:
I was just about to do that. The amendment is a simple one, to increase the inventory of stores at the end of each fiscal year from $1,250,000 to $1,600,000. When the Transport .Stores Act was passed in 1937, section 6 provided:
The inventory of stores at the end of each fiscal year after 1936-37 shall not exceed the amount of the stores inventory established as of April first, 1937, under section three of this act.
The amount of the stores inventory established on April 1, 1937, was $957,368. It was found that this section did not meet the situation, and in 1939 an amendment was sought from the house raising the amount to $1,250,000. The amendment now before the - committee seeks to place the inventory at the end of each fiscal year at an amount not to exceed $1,600,000. The hon. gentleman asks the reasons for that. The reason chiefly is the expansion in the Department of Transport. The amount of inventory when the act was passed in 1937 was $950,000, and when one compares that with the inventory to-day, namely, $1,500,000, one gets an idea of the tremendous expansion in the stores from 1937 to date. The expansion in fact has been 45 per cent. It is due particularly to the expansion of the air service branch of the Department of Transport, radio and the like. It is due also, I must admit, to prices which, as the committee knows, have increased considerably since 1937. Unless the amendment is passed the Department of Transport will not be able to abide by the terms of the section.
Mr. MaoNICOL: Just one question there. The minister said that the inventory to-day was approximately $1,500,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext:
I was in error. I wonder if I might change that. The inventory to-day is $1,374,000.
Mr. MaoNICOL: That will do for the purposes of what I have to say. I can easily understand why it might be up from $1,250,000 to $1,375,000 approximately. But is there no control to prevent those in charge of purchasing from exceeding the amount of $1,250,000 until it is now $1,375,000? I can appreciate the reasons for the increase, and that makes me ask this question. The inventory at the moment is $1,375,000 and the amendment asks for an expansion of another $225,000. It is quite conceivable that even
TMr. Chevrier.]
this amount will be passed shortly and that another amendment will be necessary providing for a further increase.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: The only reason I can give for the increase is one of expansion. In 1939 there were not the number of divisions that there are now. Civil aviation in 1939 did not have the stores it has to-day. There is a difference between purchases and stores. The stores which we have in the Department of Transport at the end of each fiscal year are in the canal division, marine division, civil aviation, meteorological and printing and stationery divisions of the Department of Transport. Each of these divisions has increased, but none of them has increased with the celerity that civil aviation and radio have, and it is because of the expansions in these divisions that it is thought necessary to increase the inventory at the end of each fiscal year.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: It is mostly price that has accounted for the increase?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: No. That is just one factor. It is mostly expansion.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Would the minister give the committee a statement as to the inventory of stores at the conclusion of the last fiscal year, so that we may have some basis of actual comparison with the figure now sought?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Yes. In order that the hon. gentleman may get the figures as I have them, on April 1, 1937, the inventory of stores was $957,000-I am not giving odd dollars and cents. To-day, by which I mean April 1, 1946, the inventory was $1,374,000 or an increase of 45 per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Has that increase been a steady ascent in the years between 1937 and 1946?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Fairly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will say if it was higher at any time than $1,374,000, or does that represent the peak at the conclusion of the fiscal year?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: That represents the peak at the conclusion of the fiscal year 1946.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext:
I did not make my
question clear. Does this represent the peak among these years for the inventory at the conclusion of a fiscal year?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext:
My recollection is no, that it does not, that at one time it was higher than the $1,374,000, but still under the $1,600,000 which w'e require here.

Transport Stores

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Would the minister say something further with reference to this expansion? He has said in general terms there has been an expansion, particularly in connection with civil aviation. Would he be a little more specific and indicate what this expansion of stores consisted of? What relation has it, for instance, to Trans-Canada Air Lines? Is any portion of this inventory related to expansion in operation of Trans-Canada Air Lines?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Yes. During the past few years the increases, as I told the hon. member for Davenport, have been confined chiefly to air services, and in air services particularly to radio and aviation materials. The table I have before me shows that the increase has been far more rapid in the meteorological and aviation divisions than in the others. The other divisions of transport have remained pretty much static. There has been a small increase but nothing to worry about. In the others the increase has been more rapid. Future civil aviation requirements are difficult to forecast. From what we know of the value of stores in aviation to-day it is felt, that all this increase will ultimately be required.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext:
Would the minister say
what was the inventory value one year before the war? As he knows, a whole lot of dilapidated stuff and junk is kept; I have seen it in yards throughout the system. Did the minister in drafting this bill have the appraisals; and what was the book value, the market value, the par value? There will be an inventory value on the books of approximately 81,600,000. Has the minister a par value and a book value of his inventory, too; are the stores replaced, and is a definite sum set aside each year in connection with this value, because it is largely a bookkeeping item? As we know, the Department of Transport has not been spending an awful lot of money during the war in this branch of its work.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asks what the value was in some year during the war. I cannot tell the hon. member. The only values I have are those in 1937 and those of to-day. But I can get the information for him. So far as par value is concerned, there is no such thing, but there is a book value, and I shall be glad to get that for him.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext:
Will the minister tell us how much of these stores at the end of April were expendable, and what was the
amount of saleable goods; what are expendable by the department and what are saleable to the services?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: They are all saleable. They can all be used and sold; there is no question about that; and as far as their expandability is concerned they are there in our stores to be used. For instance, we have seven or eight marine agencies all across Canada; one of these marine agencies is at Prescott; one is at Saint John; one is at Quebec; and the stores are there to be used by various branches of the marine agency from time to time. They are expendable at any time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: What would happen if the inventory of stores at the conclusion of a fiscal year exceeded the limit fixed by the statute?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: It is not anticipated that that position will arise, in view of the statement which I gave the committee a moment ago, because the rise has been gradual from 1937 to 1946. Even if it did rise, it could only rise in the same proportion, and this amendment relating to a maximum of $1,600,000 will certainly keep it within the confines of the act. Later, we can seek another amendment from parliament if such should be necessary. The only thing I can do is to take the opinion of the ef .crs of my department who say that this is ample for the time being and within the next few years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: They have not exceeded the limit in the past?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: No; the limit has never been exceeded.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Right now?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: No. Perhaps I should have told the committee that by virtue of P.C. 2589 of April 1, 1943, the inventory of stores was extended to 81,500,000, and that was then the financial limitation put upon the stores. So that at no time was the amount exceeded.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: With this act you can exceed it at any time by putting through an order in council?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext:
No. This act is simply giving statutory effect to what was done by order in council by virtue of the War Measures Act; and I need not tell my hon. friend that he would be the first to object strenuously if we attempted to hoist the inventory of stores by virtue of the War Measures Act, at any time. That is exactly what we do not want to do.
C.N.R.-Manitoba Railway

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Do I understand that at any time during a fiscal year the total amount might exceed this figure but it must be reduced to that at the end of a fiscal year?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: It cannot exceed this figure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: This deals with the end of a fiscal year.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: That is right. At the end of a fiscal year it cannot, if this bill passes, exceed $1,600,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: It might have been higher than that during the fiscal year?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: It was not, at any time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Suppose there is an excess of that amount; do you return these stores? Let us presume that at the end of the year the inventory was $1,700,000. What machinery has the minister to take care of a situation of that kind?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: Wj could not return the stores because they are operating stores; they are used, but we do not anticipate that that will ever arise. It has never happened since this act has been in force, since 1937.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ANNUAL MAXIMUM INVENTORY VALUE
speechtext: There may be contingencies, and you should be prepared for that, I should think.

Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of bill No. 194, respecting Canadian National Railways and the acquisition of the Manitoba railway.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Assignment of option.

When the house gave first reading to this bill I said that its object was to authorize the Canadian National Railways to purchase the railway and undertaking of the Manitoba Railway company. I went on to explain that in 1901 the Northern Pacific and Manitoba Railway company, the Winnipeg Transfer Railway company, the Portage and Northwestern Railway company and the Waskada and Northeastern Railway company leased to Her Majesty the Queen in the right IMr. ChevrierJ
of the province of Manitoba what was then known as the Manitoba Railway company for a period of 999 years, giving further in the lease an option to purchase the railway at any time during the currency of the lease for $7,000,000. Later, that lease was assigned by the province of Manitoba to the Canadian Northern Railway company. In 1901 the Canadian Northern Railway company came to parliament and obtained the authority to purchase the assignment of the lease, the railway and its undertaking and also the right to take up the option of $7,000,000. The Canadian Northern assigned its lease, and later, the Canadian Northern became a part of the Canadian National Railways, and what the Canadian National Railways seeks now is the purchase of the Manitoba railway.
The lease provides that for the first ten years the annual rental shall be $210,000; the second ten years, $225,000; the third ten years, $275,000, and the remaining period, $300,000. The Canadian National Railways has been paying that rental, but it now finds-
At which rate?

The last rate mentioned, namely, $300,000. By virtue of refinancing it finds it can borrow the money at an attractive rate of interest and save at least $90,000 a year. It has therefore sought the authority of parliament to purchase the railway.
The bill is very simple, and may be divided into four parts. First of all, it provides for the assignment of the option in accordance with the terms of the act which was passed by parliament in 1901. Second, it provides for the sale and acquisition of the railway and its undertaking, including certain stock. Third, it provides for clear title, as in any purchase; and finally, it provides for the method of effecting the transfer. That method may be subdivided into three parts. First, the Canadian National Railways may accept the purchase by means of an ordinary deed or conveyance or document under seal as one private individual would from another; or it may proceed again by expropriation as it does normally under section 17 of the Canadian National Railways Act; or it may proceed by deposit of certain plans in the land titles office of Manitoba.
The schedule to the bill provides for the length of line which is being purchased, which amounts to 353-17 miles. It provides for the purchase of seven branches of the Manitoba railway which are known as the Red River Valley railway, the Hope Farm branch, the Morris-Rrandon branch, the Souris River branch, the Portage la Prairie branch, the

C.N.R ,-Manitoba Railway
Lake branch and the Winnipeg Transfer branch; all of which totalled together make 353-17 miles.
As the committee knows, a matter such as this cannot be proceeded with unless it has the approval of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. The board of directors did give this matter consideration and by resolution approved the purchase of the railway as an excellent thing for it, first so far as refinancing was concerned and, second, so far as reduction of its fixed charges was concerned. Next, it was made the subject of discussion in the annual budget of the Canadian National Railways, and the railways and shipping committee then had an opportunity of going into this purchase. In its budget for 1946 the Canadian National Railways did provide for the sum of $7,000,000 to be set aside for this purchase. The budget of the railway for 1946 has been approved by the committee on railways and shipping.
Finally, while it may not be necessary for the railway to come to parliament for the approval of this purchase, it is felt that in a matter of this kind it is far better to obtain the best possible title that can be obtained, namely, one from parliament by an act of parliament, than by accepting a deed or by filing plans under the Expropriation Act, or by simply filing ordinary plans as set out in the last part of section 4. I think I have covered generally what I intended to say.

This particular bill has been before the country for a great many years. I object to a public ownership body, such as the Canadian National Railways, assuming all these dead-ends. The Canadian National Railways have taken over many of these provincial roads that were practically bankrupt. Now you are going to pay $7,000,000 for this one, through the purchase of stock. Some hon. members will remember the Drayton-Acworth report of 1917. The government of the day appointed a royal commission consisting of Mr. Acworth, an eminent British engineer; Sir Henry Drayton, chairman of the railway commission, and, I think, Mr. Smith, who was then president of the New York Central. They reported on the railway situation in Canada, and they found that the growth of the three transcontinental railways had far outstripped the growth of population; that there was overbuilding, and that sort oi thing, and as a result the government had to go in and save private ownership, which had failed. This was done by forming the Canadian National Railways, so called, which was supposed to be a public ownership venture.
I object to the Canadian National being loaded up with these dead-ends of provincial railways in almost eveiy province across Canada. In this case they say the property is to be conveyed free of encumbrance, and the transfer is to be effected through a straight stock deal between the vendor and the vendee. The Drayton report condemned this way of doing things. In the first place, the railway commission, now the board of transport commissioners, should have been asked to report on this propostion before anything of the kind should be recommended to this house. Then we have a committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. What are they doing? They should be looking into this question. We have another committee on railways and shipping. I can find nothing in their report about this particular railway. You know the way Mackenzie and Mann acted out west. Theirs was a political railway first, last and all the time. They came to this parliament and got tens of millions of dollars guaranteed by the government, though there was no business for their railway because it was paralleled by two others. We had a carnival of building, of reckless waste and all that kind of thing, which cost the country a tremendous sum of money.
As I understand it, this provincial railway was leased to the Canadian Northern in 1901 for some $300,000 a year. Now we have a bill before parliament to validate all the mistakes made in that particular province in regard to railways, duplication, waste of all kinds and all the rest of it. That was a sorry day for the people of this country. They are paying for it yet in high railway freight and passenger rates. We had the overcapitalization and overbuilding of railways, with three where one would have done with branch lines running off the main line. These railway magnates went into almost every province and, then, when they faced bankruptcy in 1917 the government was compelled to take over the railways. Public ownership is not to blame in this case; this shows the evils of private ownership. I repeat that in my opinion the board of transport commissioners should be asked to report on this matter before we recommend a deal like this, because for long enough the Canadian National has been loaded up with these dead, bankrupt provincial railways and these dead-ends.

I quite agree with the hon. member for Broadview that we should be very careful before taking over too many miles of railway in this country. We all remember that before the war our two great railways were going behind at the rate of thirty to forty million dollars a year. During the war,
2S16
C.N.R.-Manitoba Railway

of course, they paid their way and did a splendid job; but in these days, when we have transportation by truck, bus and other methods, we can see that the railways may not do as well in the future as they have done in the past. So that we may find ourselves carrying a heavier burden than we carried previous to the war. The hon. member for Broadview mentioned roads that have been taken over in other provinces. I know of lines that have been taken over by the Canadian National that were simply streaks of rust. I believe the committee should be told by the minister whether this is a paying proposition and what the prospects are for the future. I think we should know whether or not, to use a slang expression, the Canadian National are being sold a lemon.
I do not think I have anything further to say. During the war the railway line between Moncton and Halifax was so burdened with traffic that it was almost impossible to operate it efficiently. For a good many years they have been asking for a double track from Moncton to Halifax and from Moncton to Sydney but we could never find money for this purpose, though I think it is generally recognized as being very necessary. So I suggest to the minister that before we go on and buy up a lot of old, abandoned railways and branch lines throughout the country we spend some money in places where it is badly needed.

I am afraid I did not make myself clear, or else hon. members who have spoken are under a misapprehension. It is said that we should not take over this road, and that we should not take over old, abandoned railways. That is not what we are doing. We have this railway now whether we like it or not. We have it by virtue of a lease for 999 years, and the Canadian National has been paying rent at the rate of $300,000 a year. The hon. member for Broadview says that this is bad business, that it is not a paying proposition. I say to him that it is a paying proposition if we can reduce the annual rental which must be paid by the Canadian National from $300,000 to $210,000. We shall save $90,000 a year. There can be no doubt that this is an excellent piece of business from the point of view of both the railway and the public.
Is the railway paying?

It does not matter
whether it is paying or not; this bill has absolutely nothing to do with that. I say that because it is a necessary part of the national system whether it pays or does not pay. We are bound for 999 years. We can continue
fMr. Brooks.]
paying rent at the rate of $300,000 a year, but if we can save $90,000 a year, why not do so? That is the only object of this bill. This is not the purchase of an old, abandoned railway. This is a going concern which is operating into the city of Winnipeg from Brandon, from Portage la Prairie, from the Souris valley, from the international boundary at Emerson and from Hope Farm.
What does the minister mean when he says it is a going concern? A moment ago he told us it was not paying.

The Manitoba railway is in operation. It was operated first by the Canadian Northern, from 1901 until the Canadian Northern became part of the Canadian National. It is now part of the Canadian National Railways whether the committee likes it or not, so that I can see no merit in the argument raised by the two hon. gentlemen.

Perhaps the minister has given this information already, but could he tell the committee briefly how this lease happened to be made? Who were the contracting parties? Who	was	so	provident on	behalf ofthe dominion	as	to	enter into, a	999 year
lease?

I have already done that, but perhaps briefly I could repeat what I said, for the benefit	of	the	hon. member.	I statedat the outset	of	my	remarks that	the four
railway companies, whose names I then gave, had leased what was then known as the Manitoba Railway company, its line and undertaking, to Her Majesty the Queen in the right of the province of Manitoba for 999 years at a rental of $225,000 for the first ten years, $250,000 for the next ten years, $275,000 for the following ten years, and $300,000 for the remainder of the period.
There was contained in that lease a clause under which the railway could be purchased for the sum of $7 million during any time the lease remained unexpired. The province of Manitoba assigned the lease to the Canadian Northern. The Canadian Northern became part of the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National Railways have been paying rent for the railway and its undertaking over a number of years at the rate of $300,000 a year.
This enactment is sought, not because it is necessary to come to parliament, but because it is felt that a matter of this kind should receive from parliament its endorsation by way of an act of parliament. The saving which will be brought about through this amounts to $90,000 a year.

C.N.R .-Manitoba Railway
2S17

How is that saving
brought about?

The annual rental for the unexpired term of the 999 years is $300,000 a year. The Canadian National Railways will purchase this line for $7 million. They can borrow the $7 million at a rate of three per cent, which will mean an annual interest of $210,000.
If the Canadian National Railways own it now, why have they been paying that money?
They own the unexpired term of the lease, by way of assignment.

To whom do they pay
8300,000	a year?
They pay $300,000 a year to the Manitoba Railway company, which is a subsidiary of the Northern Pacific.
Under the lease for 999 years I take it the taxes were payable by the lessee?
I should think so, yes.
That is usually so in these case s.
I am informed it is in this one.
I take it that the Canadian National Railways are responsible 'for making good on the covenant of the lessee to pay $300,000 per annum.
Yes.

May we have a report as to what maintenance has been established, and if any replacements have been made? How many terminals are involved? As nearly as I can figure, the cost of the railway rang about $23,000 per operating mile; but if terminals are involved, that is a different matter.

The railway is in good condition. Up until December 31, 1945, the Canadian National Railways had expended $966,001, or almost a million dollars by way of capital expenditure.
Answering the second part of the hon. member's question, I would point out that there are several branches. It consists of 353-17 miles, and is made up of what is known as the Red River Valley railway, which extends from Winnipeg to the international boundary line at Emerson. It consists, further, of the Hope Farm branch, which extends from mile 47-01 to what is known as Hope Farm. It consists, further, of the Morris-Brandon branch, extending from the town of
Morris to the town of Brandon; it consists of the Souris River branch, which extends from Hartney to Belmont.
All these are connected with the Canadian National Railways?

Yes; it consists, further, of the Lake branch, from Portage la Prairie to Delta; and further, of the Winnipeg Transfer railway, which is in the city of Winnipeg, and which is a small line connecting the Canadian National Railways with the Canadian Pacific Railway in that city, for a distance of 1-21 miles.

I was more interested in
the terminals involved than in the various branches. Are there any roundhouses or shops involved?

I do not know the
answer to that question.

Are there any other
agreements of this description made with the railways?

Does the hon. member
mean the Canadian National Railways?

One can scarcely understand how an agreement of this kind, for almost a thousand years, could be made, one which commits this country for 999 years, in the sum of nearly three hundred millions of dollars. The bill before us, which saves $90,000 a year, will save in the remaining length of time between eighty-five and eighty-six millions of dollars. Surely leases of this description are almost an insult to the intelligence of parliament.
I agree that the Canadian National Railways were loaded up with a lot of iine3; and I have always felt that if we want to be fair to the national system we should examine its capital structure and see to it that we remove from it a load which it is unfair for the railway to carry, especially in view of deals of this description made in the past. In days gone by, always to the disadvantage of the Canadian National Railways, when making comparisons with the Canadian Pacific Railway company, reference has been made to the tremendous capitalization of the national system. The result was that it was impossible to make a fair comparison between the two systems.
I wonder if there are any more of these improvident agreements. A lease of this description almost staggers the imagination. Just imagine committing a country to pay nearly three hundred millions of dollars over
2S18
C.N.R -Manitoba Railway

a period of 999 years! I congratulate the company and the minister for coming to us and suggesting that the country should save between eighty-five and eighty-six millions in the remaining period of time, and stretching to a time when most of us will not be here to endure the heat of a June afternoon in the House of Commons.

Why did the railway
company not bring in a bill like this years ago? It is quite clear that if everything is according to Hoyle, as it appears to be, it is a good bill for the country.
It is.

Only two years ago the
house voted a billion dollars to the Canadian National Railways by way of wiping off debt that the railways owed the country. This bill looks like something from which the country will derive some good.

There is no question
about it. The answer is that they could not borrow money at three per cent. That is why the bill was not brought in sooner.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar raised a pertinent point when be said that this almost insults the intelligence of parliament.
I did not mean the bill; I was referring to a deal of this description.
Let me point out that parliament gave its approval in 1901 to this very lease, by virtue of chapter 53 of the revised statutes of Canada.
I was not here then.

Were the members all sober? It was still a Liberal government.
*
Parliaments change from time to time.
Has the minister in his practice ever heard of a lease that was to run for 999 years, or has he heard any other legal lights speak of such a lease?
There are plenty of them.
I am afraid I shall have to answer yes to that. I have heard of a number of such leases.

Sections 2, 3 and 4 agreed to.
