Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Soldier Settlement Act to provide that a soldier settler within the provisions of the act who served in world war II who has not abandoned his land and whose agreement has not been terminated, rescinded or assigned, and a soldier settler who did not serve in world war II who has not abandoned his land and whose agreement has not been terminated, rescinded or assigned, shall be charged in the case of the soldier settler of world war II a rate of interest of three and one-half per centum per annum in respect of his agreement made under the act after the standard date in the year 1942 or the date of his enlistment whichever is the earlier and in the case of a soldier settler who did not serve in world war II a rate of interest of three and one-half per centum per annum after the standard date in the year 1944.

Mr. Speaker, for a number of years past we have heard a lot about the sanctity of contracts, but in my opinion the contract being amended by the bill to be founded on this resolution is one of the most flagrant impositions that has been inflicted upon any group of people in Canada for quite a long number of years. I am not going to take the trouble to read the resolution, because in my opinion it should never have been placed on the order paper. It would have been much better if the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) and the government had seen fit to place on the order paper a resolution to precede a bill that would give the veterans of world war I who held contracts with the soldier settlement board on March 31, 1944, clear titles to their land. I have said what I have said, and I am going to say what I intend to say before this passes because of a solemn pledge that was made by the Prime Minister of Canada in 1917 to the members of the Canadian expeditionary force. I have placed this on the record before but I am going to do so again. One should always have a foundation for any case he wants to put forward, and for that reason I am placing this on the record once again. Sir Robert Borden had this to say:
You are men actually facing the enemy day and night. You are suffering greatly from fatigue, over-strain, and lack of rest. The marvel of it is that men could undergo such a strain without breaking; but you have never yet broken, and history will appreciate that in days to come.
You men are about to enter one of the most serious engagements that ever faced the Canadian corps. I cannot, at this moment, give any information as to where this attack will be

Soldier Settlement
staged, whether it be successful or not, it is to be borne in mind that it will not be an easy success . . . We feel confident that you will succeed where others failed: for you have never yet failed in anything you have set your hand to, as a Canadian corps.
He then went on to make certain promises in the name of this country, promises which the government of that day and this government as its successors should not hesitate to make good. However, as I see things at the present time, that is not being done. Sir Kobert Borden continued:
You can go into this action feeling assured of this, and as the head of the government, I give you this assurance; that you need have no tear that the government and the country will fail to show just appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done.
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion, that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire; and that no man, whether he goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died.
We all know that after the first great war the government of the day decided to do something for veterans who wanted to settle on the land, but from our experience and the figures I have produced here we find that they were trying to do the men who settled on the land for something. On a number of occasions we have discussed this matter in the house and I am going to place some figures on the record. I hope hon. members will not concur in the report of the special committee which was set up to deal with veterans affairs, in which report they refused to recommend clear titles. I hope they will give expression to their own honest opinions, that is, that this resolution which I shall read in a short time will be assented to and that these old settlers will be given clear title to their land.
After quite a selection had been made, the total number of settlers placed by the soldier settlement board turned out to be 25,017. The total amount advanced by way of credit to those 25,017 settlers was $109,034,331. The rate of interest charged was five per cent on current accounts and seven per cent on arrears. Perhaps I should stop here to comment on charging veterans of great war I or any other veterans an interest rate of five per cent. If we want to use it we have the sole right to issue credit on our own account, so why
should we go to some private institution and pay them a rate of interest which compels us to charge the veterans who settled under the old soldier settlement board, or those veterans who are settling under the Veterans Land Act, these high rates of interest? Five per cent is a steal from these veterans of great war I, and seven per cent on arrears is a still greater steal. This country should not tolerate steals of that kind.	[DOT]
The total amount of principal repaid at the end of March, 1944, was $50,507,493.20. I am dealing only with what was paid by soldier settlers; I am not taking into consideration the amounts paid by civilian purchasers to whom the land was sold at a much lower price than it was contracted for by the veteran settlers after they either had decided on their own accord to get off the land or were kicked off by the administration. The total interest paid was S25,381,060.13, making a total of $75,888,553.33.
I should like to refer to the conditions under which these men tried to get along. Mistakes were made in settling these men and live stock and equipment were purchased at very high prices. Because the government policy did not provide for costs of production, prices of agricultural products dropped to a very low level. The government has seen fit from time to time to cancel certain amounts of these contracts and the total cancellation of principal amounted to $24,867,637.64. Interest cancellations amounted to $19,234,239.77, making a total of cancellations of $44,101,877.41.
Then we come to the cost of administration. Somebody has been trying to put across the idea that the cost of administration runs to only $100,000 a year, but the figures brought down in the house showed that the cost of administration up to the end of March, 1944, was $27,340,763.64. That is the cost of administration of the soldier settlement part only of this board from the inception of the scheme. That works out to an average annual cost of $1,100,000 for administration.
Going a little farther, we find that at the end of March, 1944, the total amount outstanding so far as the soldier settlers were concerned was $7,715,954.01. The total amount of arrears at that time was $1,054,269.30-I am still speaking only of the soldier settlement part of the programme. At that time 6,153 soldier settlers remained on the land; that is approximately 25 per cent of the original number. The average original amount of credit advanced to the settlers was $4,358.40. The average balance of debt of the settlers on March 31, 1944, was $1,254. That is equal to 29 per cent of the original amount of credit advanced.
Soldier Settlement

The number who acquired title during that 25-year period was 4,130, or approximately 16 per cent of the original settlers who made contracts with the government. I think there are in this house a number of business men; and I am going to ask any one of them, even the poorest business man in the house, whether that is a good business proposition and whether under those conditions they would force these settlers to continue to carry on, persecuting still further these soldier settlers of world war I.
Before going farther, may I state that the settlers who are now being settled under the Veterans Land Act, taking advantage of the full amount of the grant and engaging in fulltime farming, receive $2,320 by way of grant. This amounts to 39 per cent of the total credit extended.
The settlers I have spoken of owe at the present time only 29 per cent of their original credit. Those of us who have been in the house for some little time realize that the settlers have been trying to do something for themselves for a long time. Back in 1936, in Lloydminster, which is within thirty miles of my home, the soldier settlers' union was formed; and in 1938, as a result of their work, a brief was presented by the union to the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, of which I hold a copy in my hand. On the outside cover I find this:
To the Honourable the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada
Honourable Sirs,
In presenting this brief, our endeavour has been to draw attention to our unavailing efforts to bring about a conference between government officials and representatives of returned men on the land, which will have as its result the permanent solution of the soldier settlement problem without imposing on the taxpayer of this country further large expenditures, as occasioned in the past by abortive relief measures.
We submit that the evidence contained herein will be found, by any impartial investigation, to be conclusive in support of their claims, and we respectfully request that they be given every consideration by the government, which will lead to a conference at which all soldier organizations interested in soldier settlement be fully represented to bring about a permanent solution to the soldier settlement problem, based on the recommendations of the soldier settlers' union convention. 1936, and the resolution passed at the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion, 1936.
Most respectfully yours,
R. J. Stewart, President,
H. G. Mitchell, Vice-President,
H. S. Packman, General Secretary, Soldier Settlers' Union.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

When the house took recess at six o'clock I had just stated that for a number of years the old soldier settlers have been making attempts in vain to have something worth while done to relieve them of the load of debt which was placed upon them by the different governments since the end of the first great war. I also placed on record the introduction to a brief which was presented to the Senate and the House of Commons by the soldier settlers' union away back in January, 1938. Nothing of course was done at that time, and the settlers were disappointed then as they have been disappointed ever since. In 1939 the second great war broke out. At that time a number of old settlers were still badly in arrears, and the soldier settlement board, realizing that sooner or later it would probably be called upon to perform another duty, in the way of settling another group of veterans after the war which began in 1939 was concluded, decided that they had better start in and clean up the mess, get rid of some of the land and also get rid of some of the settlers on the land who were not able to make their payments.
Some people do not believe that this government and previous governments have taken any action to dispossess old veterans of the first great war; but the record shows that, from 1930 to 1942 inclusive, 1,006 settlers signed quit-claim deeds, and during the same period nearly 1,000 were served with thirty-day notices to get off or pay up. In most cases the settlers had to get off, because they did not have the wherewithal to pay up. We have been told that in the case of those who signed quit-claim deeds the action was as a rule taken voluntarily, but I believe that anyone who takes the trouble to investigate many of these cases will find that plenty of pressure was applied to make these men sign quit-claim deeds. That was common knowledge at the time. After the last war broke out, many of these old settlers sent their sons and daughters overseas to do the fighting so that Canada could continue to live in peace and prosperity, while they themselves were producing food, working as many as sixteen hours a day in food production; yet between April 1, 1942, and March 31, 1943, the board had 253 settlers sign quit-claim deeds, and 108 settlers were served with thirty-day notices to get off or pay up. This is the treatment which was handed out to men who, after having done their best, in many cases were not able to make good, not because of con-

Soldier Settlement
ditions over which they had any control but because of prices they had to pay at the beginning and because of an agricultural policy which was not in the interests of the producers. As a result these same veterans were thrown out in the gutter who went over between 1914 and 1918 and helped to keep Canada on the map under the union jack.
Then again we find that after the second world war broke out, numbers of these settlers who were in sufficiently good health to serve in that war found themselves under such a load of debt that they were not able to make a living for	their	wives	and families,	anddecided to enlist a second time and offer their lives if needs be as a sacrifice. The government, finding that these men had left and that in	some	cases	the land was	notbeing farmed properly, and finding that in some cases it was so poor that it could not produce enough to pay the taxes and accrued interest, passed, on the advice of the former minister of mines and resources under whose direction the soldier settlement board was then administered, an order in council so that the interests of the board would be protected. The order in council was passed on March 19, 1941, and is	known	as P.C. 138-1936. It	hadthe effect of	taking	away	the very bread	and
butter from the wives and families of the veterans of the first great war, veterans who were not able to keep up their payments and who had gone overseas to fight again. Lest there should be any misunderstanding I am going to read the effective part of the order in council. It is as follows:
Accordingly the hoard recommend that notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained in any of the regulations providing for payment of dependents' or marriage allowance in respect of dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces, that in all cases where the dependents of an enlisted person continue to occupy the farm for which such person is indebted to the director of soldier settlement and in respect of which the contract terms are not otherwise satisfactorily provided for, there may be deducted from the dependents' or marriage allowance amounts sufficient to provide for payment of taxes levied by the local taxing authority in respect of the property in question and interest accruing annually on indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement, such deductions to be made monthly and in no case to exceed $20 per month except with the consent of the dependents concerned.
Shame.
It is a shame. He ought to be ashamed of himself.

That is the stand taken by this government, the government which claims credit for the good things it is doing for the veterans of this war. What has it done for
the veterans of the first great war? Remembei that the men for whom I am speaking are also veterans of this war; that is, those who were lucky enough to come back. The government, in order to satisfy the treasury board, perhaps, and our monetary greed, takes away from the wives and families of those men who were over there fighting, the wherewithal which was provided by the government in order that these wives and families might live at least in decency while their men were away. Very fine treatment, indeed!
Again, a little later on we find that another order in council was passed whereby those settlers who were still in debt could make application to a board which was set up to have the terms of their agreement extended for another twenty years and also to have their indebtedness reduced. What is the effect of that? In the first instance the contract was for twenty-five years, and with the additional twenty years it means forty-five years that the settler must serve and pay the soldier settlement board a price far in excess of the value of the land and equipment he received. He has the opportunity to do that for the sake of what? That is praise for having gone over and fought in the first and second great wars. It is a shame that any government should impose a penalty of that kind on its soldiers.
Knowing these conditions, the soldier settlers could not carry on because our wheat prices until August, 1942, were down to seventy cents a bushel, f.o.b. Fort William, which is below fifty cents on the farm in western Canada. This is a price which did not exist previously except for a short time in the depths of the depression. The soldier settlers could not carry on. In April, 1943, they met at Saskatao-n to try to do something for themselves. In November. 1943. they held another meeting at Saskatooon and at that time they decided to circulate a petition to have clear titles granted. No expenses were incurred in the circulation of that petition so far as the government was concerned. Veteran settlers and civilians alike took copies of the petition, drove around the country over snow-blocked roads, obtained signatures to the petition and at the same time collected dimes and nickels from people in order that a delegation might come to Ottawa to present the petition.
On May 23. 1944, a delegation of nine representatives from that organization presented a brief to six members of the cabinet here in Ottawa, presided over by the then minister of mines and resources, who is now in another place enjoying all the cream which can be provided for him. These members were cordially received, and after having
Soldier Settlement

been given a fine reception and told that their request would receive sympathetic consideration the men went home feeling that at last they were going to have some justice meted out to them. I may say that was before the election took place. We expected an election that fall, and honeyed words were handed out at the time. The house was in session until August of that year, and no report was made to the house by the responsible minister. But some of us had hardly got home when an announcement came over the radio and was issued in the press that the government would not grant this request. At the time the delegation came to Ottawa we found that, the director of the soldier settlement board had inserted in The Legionary-I think with the permission and perhaps on the instructions of the then minister of mines and resources-a report dealing with these clear titles, setting out in detail one side of the case, which, I might say, has been torn to ribbons in this house since that time. The concluding paragraph of his remarks reads as follows: The gentleman to whom I am refering is none other than Mr. Murchison, the director of the soldier settlement board. He said:
In conclusion I am authorized to say that the proposal is not deemed to be in the public interest and, consequently, it is not being entertained by the government. Therefore, the best advice I can offer to the soldier settlers concerned is to get into step with those who manifestly prefer securing title to their farms by complying with the terms of their agreements.
Who is he?
He is the director.
I thought he was a Hitler.

The man with whom the new veterans will have to deal unless something necessary is done.
Then, feeling that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) did not know of the treatment which was being handed out to these old veterans, I made a special trip to Ottawa and visited the Prime Minister early in October, 1944. The Prime Minister listened carefully to what I had to say. I left a copy of the case with him, and he told me then that within a week or so the new Department of Veterans Affairs would be set up headed 'by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs and that he would turn the matter over to him. Having had conversation with the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), I felt that at last we were going to get a square deal for the old veterans. The department was set up and no clear titles were forthcoming. Therefore, in March, 1945, the president and secre-
TMr. Fair.]
tary of the soldier settlers' association accompanied me to Ottawa. We visited the Minister of Veterans Affairs and had quite a long talk with him. We presented our case and he listened attentively. Then he gave us objections which were prepared for him, I believe, by the director because the words of the director were in the statement of the minister. They were to the effect that payments and pre-payments were being made; that if titles were granted to old soldiers the new veterans would not pay, and so forth. Payments and pre-payments were being made for a great many reasons. The sons and daughters of these old settlers had gone overseas. Some of them had gone to work in war factories. Some of them were receiving dependents' allowances on account of their sons and daughters who had enlisted. As a result of pressure, and plenty of it, which was being put on by the board, these old soldiers turned in every penny they could get hold of. As a result payments were coming in freely, and that is the way things were going. We were told that if titles were granted to the old soldiers the new soldiers would not pay. I wish to advise the government now that if they impose on the new veterans conditions such as were imposed on the old veterans we shall have a revolution in this country before long. Make no mistake about that. They may blame the communists for it, too, but they are the ones who will be to blame if these conditions occur once more.
Then we went to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in connection with the same request, and he also told us that payments were coming in freely, and that he. believed in the sanctity of contracts. All these old veterans believe in the sanctity of contracts and they proved it by going overseas to fight for the country which is giving them their living. They came back and they were sold land, live stock and equipment at prices far in excess of their value. In my home district one halfsection was sold1 by a father to his son for $8,000 at a time -when prevailing prices of land in the territory were $1,000 to $1,200 for a quarter section. Needless to say, that land is not yet paid for.
When the government made the contract with these old settlers it was made on the basis of prices which existed at that time. We might say that during the years after the war wheat went up to $2.50 to $3 a bushel. Later, we find that the settlers were compelled to pay their debts when wheat went down as low as cents at Wininpeg. That meant a breaking of the contract by the government. When they sold land, equipment and live stock to these men they should have seen to it that

Soldier Settlement
prices were upheld. Proper floor prices should have been established until these things were paid for. That was not done, and yet the Minister of Finance believes that contracts should be maintained and honoured. We believe that too.
Some of our bureaucrats say that this is just the request of a few disgruntled veterans around Saskatoon. I want to contradict that statement flatly. The petition which was circulated contained some 12,500 signatures and was representative of the three prairie provinces. The request for clear title was also supported by the Alberta legislature, the Saskatchewan legislature, the Alberta farmers' union, the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities, the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, United Farmers of Alberta, the Alberta branch of the Canadian Legion, the executive of the British Columbia branch, and last, but not least, the dominion command of the Canadian Legion. In order that there may be no question as to the authenticity of these, I should like to read just one or too At a meeting of the Alberta provincial council, held in Edmonton from June 6 to June 9, 1943, the soldier settlers' committee presented a report, and the resolution adopted was as follows:
Whereas the majority of original soldier settlers, who are still endeavouring to carry on under the soldier settlement scheme have now found it, owing to advanced years and the adverse conditions prevailing in agriculture, particularly the lack of parity prices, increasingly difficult to liquidate their indebtedness to the settlement board.
And whereas the settlers have struggled on through the years of drought conditions and low prices unprecedented in the agricultural history of this country and have now nothing to show for. their years of toil and struggle but whatever equity they may have in the land which is liable to foreclosure.
Therefore be it resolved that we now petition the government to relieve the soldier settlers of any further payments and that they be given the title deed to their land or, failing this, that a parliamentary committee in eoniunetion with representation from the dominion command of the Canadian Legion, review the whole situation of the soldier settlers with a view to alleviating their present financial difficulties.
That resolution was sent here, but of course nothing was done about it. Then not very long ago, on October 26 of last year, the head of the Canadian Legion, Mr. Alex. Walker, presented a brief to the committee on veterans affairs, and under the heading "Soldier Settlement Act" he had this to say:
The bill under consideration lowering the interest rate for soldier settlers under the Soldier Settlement Act of 1919 meets one of the recommendations of the soldier settlement report of the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion
held in Vancouver in June, 1944, in that it proposes to lower the interest from 5 per cent to 3J per cent.
A further proposal recommended by this committee relates to the granting of clear titles to aged settlers or to those who had reduced their indebtedness to 25 per cent of the original purchase price. A great deal of discussion has been carried on during the past few years respecting soldier settlers of the last war and strong representations, from time to time, have been made from various sources to solve the problem of these veterans by granting them clear title to their farms. A debate occurred in the House of Commons recently on this subject and many members spoke in favour of the proposal. Representations by soldier settlers through the legion have followed similar lines and the following resolution is submitted for the consideration of this committee:
Therefore be it resolved that, in order to be fair to our ageing veterans and to bring the old and the new settlement acts more into line, the dominion government be asked to readjust the debts of the 6,153 original soldier settlers who have not paid for their lands, such readjustment to take into consideration the difference in interest rates charged under the said acts; and that following such readjustment the government be further asked to cancel the debts of those original soldier settlers whose debt has been, or may hereafter be, reduced to 25 per cent of the original purchase price or the reduced purchase price.
Right here I would say that if consideration were given to the difference between the interest rates charged the new veterans and the old veterans, all these old settlers would have been out of debt many years ago. After that brief was completed, the hon. member for Acadia had this to say, at page 315 of the proceedings of that committee:
On page 11 of the brief there is a reference to the old soldier settlers, and the recommendation there is that clear title be given provided a soldier reduces his indebtedness to 25 per cent of the original purchase price of the reduced purchase price. I do not think that will go far enough to satisfy the organization that calls itself the old soldier settlers' organization, because they are asking for a clear title for all soldier settlers of the last war. I think we must all agree that the soldiers who are in the most difficult position of all are those soldier settlers who have had no chance of reducing their indebtedness to that 25 per cent, the ones who have been up against bad luck. Some of you may call it bad management, perhaps, but we know that the situation these men went through in the depression years put them in a position where they could not get the money to buy the farm. I should like very much to see that 25 per cent taken out of your recommendation, making it wide open so that title can be given to the old soldier settlers, whether in the fortunate position of being able to reduce their indebtedness to 25 per cent or not. I wonder if Mr. Walker would comment on that?

feelings if you do give them clear title.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak on this resolution, but rather to speak on second reading of the bill. However, in view of the debate which has developed, I feel I must say a few words.
The resolution has been on the order paper since April 12, and we were beginning to think it was going to be almost a fixture. The committee on veterans affairs has been sitting for forty days or more, during which time it has had many matters before it. Very little from that committee has been brought to the house, for which possibly there is a good reason.
However, I am pleased indeed that at last a subject has been placed before the house, and that we shall have something definite to show for our work. This matter, in itself, is not contentious. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) has criticized it, not on the ground of what it does, but rather on the ground of what it does not contain. As I have said, there was unanimous consent in the veterans affairs committee in respect of the matter contained in the resolution itself.
As hon. members will see, the proposed bill ratifies two orders in council which were passed some months ago. As a matter of fact one was passed in November, 1942, and the other in March, 1945. The intention of the bill is simply to ratify these two orders in council.
P.C. 10472 provided for two things. It authorized the director of the soldier settlement board, with the approval of the treasury board, to make capital reduction in the debt of certain soldier settlers. This, as we know, has been done. I believe there has been a reduction in the debt of old settlers to an extent of something like a million to a million and a quarter dollars. There is general approval among the soldiers and, I am sure, among civilians as well, from one end of Canada to the other, of that procedure.
The other provision in order in council P.C. 10472 was a reduction in the interest rate from five per cent to 3i per cent. This, too, has general approval.
Veterans are now taking up land under the Veterans Land Act. They are borrowing money and having land allotted to them on the provision of paying 3^ per cent. Strong representations were made to the government in 1942 that the interest rate charged the old settler should be the same as that charged the new settler under the Veterans Land Act. This also is provided for in the bill, and was given unanimous approval by the veterans affairs committee.
Order in council P.C. 8346 not only provides that the old soldier shall have a reduction in his interest rate from five per cent to 3J per

Soldier Settlement

cent, but also provides that all settlers under the Soldier Settlement Act shall be treated in the same way. So that there is a general reduction in the interest rate from five per cent to 3i per cent. I might say that this, too, has received the unanimous approval of the veterans affairs committee. It also fixes the date upon which this reduction of interest is to take effect, namely either the date upon which the soldier settler enlisted, or 1942, whichever is the earlier date.
I do not think it is necessary to make further comment because, as I say, there was unanimous consent in the committee. However, since the hon. member for Battle River has introduced the question of giving clear title to old soldiers I feel that as one of the members of the committee I should say a few words on the subject. First, I wish to commend the hon. member not only for his action upon this occasion but also for his actions in the past six or seven years, during ft'hich time he has fought what he and a good many others of us consider to be the battle of the old soldier. He is to be congratulated upon the interest he has taken.
The hon. member has mentioned that this matter was discussed by the veterans affairs committee for a considerable length of time. I do not think it is incumbent upon me to review the different arguments used by hon. members. Thie ground has been thoroughly covered by the hon. member for Battle River this evening, as it was covered in his former speeches.
I have felt that we might very well give special consideration to the old soldiers who took up their land'in 1919 and 1920 and who for the last twenty-five or twenty-six years have been struggling to pay off their debt. It has seemed to me that, now that, they have reached ages ranging from fifty-five to eighty years, we might give them some consideration.
We are told by Mr. Murchison, .director of the Veterans Land Act, that there was now due from these old soldier settlers something less than So million. In 1919 there were some 25.000 soldiers of the last war, men who had come back from overseas who were anxious to take up farms in this country, but to-day there are only 4,276 of those still remaining on their farms. They have paid many millions of dollars off their indebtedness to the soldier settlement board. As was pointed out this afternoon, they worked under terrible handicaps. First, they went through the great war. Next, they took over farms when prices were greatly inflated and they had to buy cattle at the rate of $100 to $150 a head. Prices of farm machinery were much more than they were in normal times. Be-

sides that, these old soldiers passed through the worst depression this country has ever known. From 1929 to 1938 Canada, along with the rest of the world, passed through a depression unknown to any other generation. Then along came the second great war. Many of these men enlisted for service and those who did not had sons and1 daughters enlisting in the service. Taking all these things into consideration, I submit that these men have a strong claim upon the generosity of the people of this Dominion of Canada.
When we compare it with the billions and hundreds of millions of dollars that are passed through this house, five million dollars is a small sum to pay for the sacrifices that these men have made during the past twenty-five years. This would not be a total loss. As the hon. member pointed out, we are paying for the supervision and direction of the soldier settlement board a sum amounting to well over $100,000 a year. The hon. member for Battle River said that it has cost 827,000 000 to administer the Soldier Settlement Act. I doubt if it is costing anywhere near that sum to-day, but there is no doubt that it is costing well over $100,000. If we washed out these debts and gave clear title to these men we would not be losing any great amount of money because we would save in the cost of administering this act.
As I pointed out a few moments ago, many of these men served in the last war and many of their sons and daughters have served. Some of these men are now sixty, seventy or even eighty years of age. They have lived on their farms for twenty-five years. What man living on a farm for twenty-five years has not the hope that before he passes on to the Great Beyond he will be able to leave a clear title to his land to his widow and children? It would be impossible for these men to do that at the present time. They are too old to make a success of farming. Without going into the arguments which have been so well advanced, I submit that we could afford to be generous to these men to that extent.
As far as the committee was concerned, we were not unanimous in turning this down. I think the vote was seventeen to twenty-one, and I was one of those who supported the motion of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). If it had not been that the government brought in what I would term their tactical reserve for the vote it would have been carried in the committee and there would have been a direct recommendation from the committee that these old soldiers be given clear title. I am not going to labour the point any further because I do not think it requires any additional argument.

There are some other matters I should like to mention while I am on my feet. One of these is brought to my mind by an article which appeared some time ago in the Globe and Mail. As I said at the beginning, there have been very few opportunities in this house during the past five or six weeks to bring up veterans affairs. This particular matter has reference to a soldier who joined up in September, 1939. He spent five years in the army and, while overseas, took four courses in agriculture. He hoped that when he came back to Canada he would be able to get a farm in this country and follow the vocation for which he had prepared himself and which he liked. When he came back to Canada he did obtain a farm. After seven months he found that it was impossible to get the loan under the Veterans Land Act for which he had hoped.
I do not want to criticize the director of the Veterans Land Act because I do not think there is an official in any department of government who is worked harder. Not only is he overworked, he is an harassed man. As my hon. friend has said, the conditions imposed upon these men made it almost an impossibility for them to make a success of their farming. They could not sell a cow or a pig; they could not buy a piece of machinery; they could not turn around without having to consult a representative of the soldier settlement board. Let us be careful this time. This letter from a young soldier which appeared in the Globe and Mail indicates that there is a tendency along that line. We should watch ourselves. I warn the minister and the department to be careful to see that technicalities do not interfere with the proper administration of the act.
For instance, a man who has been overseas may want to take up farming. He is told that his wife must be interviewed, but his wife may still be in England. She may have to remain there for five or six months and during that time the man will be unable to get a farm. His wife must be interviewed, I suppose given the once-over as we say, by the officials administering the act. These things react against the success of this scheme. Again I say to the minister that he should be careful to see that such things are not carried to an extreme. I brought up this matter of the letter which was reported in the Globe and Mail because there was an editorial in that paper, not only condemning the government but condemning the opposition because matters of this kind are not brought before the house and because there is no general airing of these matters before parliament.
Along the same line I have received a letter from a legion representative in Nova Scotia protesting the appointment of legal representatives to search titles and do other general legal work under the Veterans Land Act who have not seen any service at all. That is absolutely contrary to what we understand is the policy of the government.

A delegation of old soldier settlers came to Ottawa in 1944 and interviewed some members of the cabinet. These soldier settlers were assured that their problems would be given sympathetic consideration. Of course, that was before an election. In the committee the other day the minister made this statement:
As long as I am in charge of the administration, I will not stand for the destruction of that principle.
The principle he was speaking of was the principle of granting to these old soldier settlers clear title to their homes, as they should be granted.
The only principle involved here is the principle of justice. These men, if that principle had been observed, would have been granted clear title long ago. They were settled on land, as has been explained by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), under conditions where there was no possible chance of them succeeding. I know those conditions. I have lived amongst these men. I know the struggle they put up over the years to meet their obligations. In 1940, when I first came to this house I spoke to certain members of the soldier settlement board, and they told me that many of these old soldier settlers who had not paid their debts and are still on the land are the hard core of those who, the implication was, would under no circumstances meet their obligations. Yet in 1944 over 95 per cent of these men whom the officials of the soldier settlement board said were the hard core of those, who had no intention of meeting their obligations w'ere meeting them because economic conditions in the country had changed and made it possible for them to do so. These men had to struggle for years against circumstances over which they had no control. What would any hon. member do if he had to make a choice between educating his family and meeting his payments? I know one of these soldier settlers on a quarter-section of land. He had three boys and two girls, very bright children indeed. He had to make a choice between meeting his obligations to the board and giving his children a chance to go to high school. He gave his children that chance. He sent them to high school and he was unable to meet his obligations to the board. What happened? A few years later, when this country needed men, two of these boys responded to the call to the colours and joined the flying corps and one of them did not come back from overseas. Did that father not serve his country better by giving

his children their chance for an education than if he had met his obligations to the board?
There is now a small group of these soldier settlers left who, because of adverse circumstances, for family reasons perhaps, sickness, drought, poor land or other circumstances over which they had no control, have not been able to meet their obligations. Surely to-day the people of Canada can afford to give them clear title to their land.
There was no unanimity in the committee about bringing in this measure.

That the write-down of the indebtedness of soldier settlers, as recommended by the committee, provide that the settler be granted an equity of 33J per cent of the 1940-41 value of his land, irrespective of any payments made to him.

speechtext: I believe there will be a bill brought before the house on the Veterans Land Act. I suggest that the session is running on long enough without having two debates on the Veterans Land Act. I quite agree. I was simply trying to make a comparison to prove that we have more inflation to-day than we had when the old settlers were settled. I am thoroughly convinced that the units in Charleswood, which I have spoken of are not worth 50 per cent of the cost put into them on a cost-plus basis. I have inspected them and gone through them with the settlers.
I shall return to my original argument. As has been so well said, stock and equipment cost these old settlers a great deal in 1919 and 1920, following the last war. In other sessions I have given concrete examples in my own community. One of these settlers failed during the drought periods and signed a quit-claim deed to the board. He had agreed to pay approximately 85,000 for his halfsection, which is around 815 an acre. He did not have a chance to re-buy that farm when it was re-sold. It was sold to a citizen, a speculator, who was not even a British subject at that time-but that does not matter- for less than 8500, less than 10 per cent of what the original settler had agreed to pay for the farm; but the board would not give the settler a chance to buy the farm. In fact, if rumours are correct the same speculator is endeavouring to sell that farm back to the board to-day. I point that out as one of the examples of what the settlers had to contend with through no fault of their own. I thought that was unfair at that time. That is what we have been doing, and we are now in an inflationary period despite what the indices show-
The hon. member and his party want to remove the price ceilings.

I think we can still make these adjustments for these old settlers. May I ask the hon. member for Vancouver North, who has been so keen to take part in this discussion, if he is opposed to giving further adjustments to these old settlers?

It is not a case of further adjustments. May I ask the hon. member a question? If you cancel these loans to the old settlers how are you going to collect the present loan to the settlers under the Veterans Land Act?

I was making that very argument, that already under the small holdings units an order in council has been passed to write off 81,000,000 without the settler having a contract to purchase these homes. This write-off is being made before they are in there.
That is an adjustment, not a cancellation. There is a great difference between an adjustment and a cancellation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That has nothing to do with this bill. Why hold up this bill which reduces interest?
You are better on the black market than you are on this.
I have never been closer to the black market than the hon. member for Vancouver North. In fact, I do not profess to know as much about it as he does. The point is this. My hon. friend-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the house that it is necessary to have some limit to the interruptions.

The point is that today these settlers are given a grant of 82,300 and some odd if they fulfil their contract, which was not the case with the old settlers. My argument is that the old settlers are entitled to at least as much as the present veterans, because in something over 90 per cent of the cases their families did make a great contribution in the recent war. They are the type of citizens who should be encouraged in this country to-day; and without repeating other arguments that have been advanced, I may say that at the proper time I am going to support the hon. member for Battle River and continue this fight until these old settlers receive a better deal for themselves and their dependents.

It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and has been for some considerable time that the veterans who were settled under the old act of 1919 and who are still indebted to the federal treasury should be granted clear title to these lands as of March 31, 1944. In the first place, as has been said already to-night, when the loans were made no gifts were made to these veterans, as

Soldier Settlement
is being done to-day. Under the Veterans Land Act of 1942 a gift of $2,320 is made; and if that gift had been made to the veterans in 1919 I doubt if there would be any indebtedness whatever against their land to-day. After twenty-seven years of struggle with the elements and the federal treasury these people are still in debt. To-day, as has been indicated, the gift from the treasury amounts to 39 per cent of the loan. We will admit that some concessions have been made to these old veterans of world war I, in the matter of reduction of principal and reduction of arrears, but that will hardly compensate for a gift of 39 per cent of the original indebtedness.
In the second place, the interest rate on veterans' farm loans of 1919 was five per cent, with seven per cent charged on arrears. This was another factor which militated against the ability of these veterans to meet their obligations and reduce their indebtedness. The rate to-day of 3J per cent under the Veterans Land Act is still too high, but it would have enabled the veterans of the first war, had it been applied to their contracts, to meet their instalments without so much difficulty. Had the gift been granted, together with the lower rate of interest, on the loans of 1919 it is probable that there would b'e no demand to-day for cancellation of debts, since those debts would have been liquidated long ago.
It has been suggested that it would be unfair to the soldier settlers who have obtained clear title to their land to wipe out the indebtedness against the 4,200 parcels on which the debt is still outstanding. We have three soldier settlers in the house, at least three to whom I have spoken, though there may be more. Those three, all of whom have paid off their indebtedness, are in favour of cancellation of debt for these other unfortunate veterans. I cannot accept the view that any of the veterans who have paid off their indebtedness would be opposed to a fair deal being offered to veterans still in debt. I have not yet run across any who hold that view; I have yet to find a single man with a clear title who takes that attitude. Why should they? These men were comrades in arms. Some have been a little more fortunate than others. Some obtained good land, while others were placed on poor soil. It was not any fault of theirs. Some had good fortune, with substantial crops over a period of years, while others had misfortune dog their path year after year, with poor crops owing to drought, hail, pests and so on; and frequently they had family illnesses which held them back. To say that by cancellation of the debt on these particular lands we would not be 63260-179*
treating these settlers all alike is probably true, but we have never treated them all alike. Had they all obtained good land in 1919, the story to-day would be different. They are not treated all alike to-day, either. Some receive university grants which in all probability will run into thousands of dollars. That is an excellent thing, but other young veterans are only receiving the civil reestablishment grants amounting to a few hundred dollars. We are not treating them all alike to-day; and we did not treat them all alike in 1919. To argue that we must treat these veterans all alike sounds very fine, but the fact is that this has never been done.
The veterans who are requesting clear title to their lands have laboured for twenty-five years and more to obtain that title. We should not concern ourselves particularly with regard to those who have been fortunate enough to secure clear title. Our concern must be for the old veteran or his widow, who is still struggling to secure a clear title. It is a race against time. Their average age is around sixty, while a few are in the eighties. To illustrate how the old settlers feel about this matter may I quote from a letter I received from one of them out in Saskatchewan:
I served in France and Belgium in the first world war. Came home to find that while I was in hospital . . .-a hospital in England- my half-section had been sold to a German. One-quarter was my homestead and I owed for part of the other. I had to start all over again with the soldier settlement board.
I am in my seventieth year and after twenty-five years I find myself still owing the soldier settlement board almost a thousand dollars. I would like to have the satisfaction of having my land clear before I die, but if I continue to have hailed and dried out crops as in the past, I can expect to have a supervisor come and ask me to sign a quit-claim as others have had to do.
My only two sons volunteered and gave their services in this war. I have worked hard for them all these years and feel that I have surely earned the deed of my land.
No doubt all hon. members have received similar letters. Most of these settlers were industrious enough, but misfortune came their way. By granting them clear title to-day we would be righting a wrong and rectifying a grave injustice which has been allowed to continue altogether too long. It has been objected that to grant these clear titles would involve $5,000,000 in cancelled debts. When one considers that the administrative cost of the Soldier Settlement Act has exceeded $27,000,000, the $5,000,000 does not appear so very great. Neither does it seem so great when one considers that we expended much more than $5,000,000 a day during the last war. But now we are at peace, Mr. Speaker; the story is different, and unfortunately our attitudes are different. If this country is
Soldier Settlement

spending too much money in some respects or under certain departments, let us practise economy, but not at the expense of these old veterans. I feel we owe them a great deal; so let us give them justice now.
It has been said also that by granting clear titles administration of the Veterans Land Act would be made more difficult, and I have heard it said that young veterans of world war II would take advantage of the situation and stall in their payments, so that twenty-seven years from now they might get title from a humanitarian government of that day. I have too high a regard for these young veterans to think they would take advantage of a situation brought about by the misfortune of these elder veterans. More than that, it seems most ridiculous to me that anyone would wish to carry a burden of debt for twenty-seven years, just in the hope of getting clear title in the year 1973.
I am convinced that free title should be granted to every one of these old soldier settlers, or to their widows, who are still owing money to the federal treasury. It is t.he duty of all of us to give this subject our careful consideration. If that be done, I am certain we shall do justice to the old soldier settlers of a generation ago, who are fast disappearing from the scene.
Mr. J. 0. PROBE: (Regina City): Mr. Speaker, I have not spoken often during this session-
An lion. MEMBER: A pity.

Last autumn there was sent to me a series of photographs of homes of soldier settlers who had taken advantage, as they thought at that time of the settlement scheme following the first world war. I do not intend to show these photographs to hon, members, but I should be very glad if some of them who have not yet realized that these men have had to battle against untold difficulties and disappointments, would come up to my office and take a look at them. I have had them posted on the walls of my room for some months, as a reminder to me that I have a job to do 'here on their behalf.
However, I intend to read to hon. members the captions which appear over these various photographs. The heading on the frame on which the photographs are posted is in these words:

Soldiers' homes after twenty-five years of the worst kind of drudgery, coupled with an endless battle with hail, wind, drought and grasshoppers.
And with true soldier-settler wit we find repeated on the second line the statement by Sir Robert Borden following the last war:
Our soldiers shall never want after fighting so gallantly; the pledge of Sir Robert Borden for Canada; will it be honoured now?
Attached to these sheets are ten photographs showing ten soldiers' homes in one district. These are not in my constituency, and I am not now speaking from any political desire to obtain votes. This does not concern me particularly, because mine is an urban constituency. Opposite the first photograph is this caption:
No. 1 is the home of Frank Smith, who had to move out and make a living elsewhere.
What a hovel it appears! Then:
No. 2 is the home of Hugh De Blaquire, a man who was very badly wounded, and a 100 per cent pensioner. There is no water on his place, caused by the indifference of the board. The soldier settlement board even tried to compel him to make payments out of his pension.
No. 3 is where Herbert Darling was first located on a very poor quarter. The hole in the ground indicated by the arrow was where he lived for ten years. The bottom of an old bundle rack-
A hay rack, to any who are not farmers.
-formed the roof of his abode, while the sides were any old rough lumber. Eventually two of his good neighbours assisted him financially to purchase No. 8 where he now lives. Darling is a very good worker but has had very bad luck. He was severely kicked in the face by a horse.
No. 4 is the home of Ronald McDonnell, a front-line man. He and his wife and three children had to exist in this hovel.
I hope some of the members will look at it some time.
The soldier settlement board even tried to sell his place away from him while he was away trying to make a dollar on the side.
No. 5 is Y. Castiglioni's home. This is the worst ease of all. Eight children were raised in this hovel. There is only a quarter-section with 30 acres of waste land on the quarter. After being hailed out, dried out and blown out over a period of twelve years he was put off with a very sick wife and three children of school age. The soldier settlement board knew he had no place to go. This is the most dastardly piece of business on record.	-
No. 6 is the home of George Lobbans, a frontline man. This is a disgrace to Canada.
The picture here would indicate that that is no overstatement.
No. 7 is the abode of R. Hunter, another frontline man. After being hailed out five times in succession he was evicted because he refused to pay the board his last dollar.
Then, Nos. 8 and 3 were described in connection with No. 3.
No. 9 is the McNaughton home-

A family of five lived in this dump.
No. 10 is Mike Robins' home, a front-line man and very badly wounded. This is how Canada shows her appreciation for another veteran. Surely there are some gallant gentlemen in our house of parliament.

I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I think he will agree with me when I say that he should not go into details on the resolution. I am heartily in agreement with every word that you say and I congratulate you upon making your case so clear. What I was trying to do was to discuss the principle of this matter. As I say, when we have calamities at home in the form of drouth which affect a large section of our people there is a demand made nationally for a pound of flesh. But when there is a calamity far away -and I happen to know the extent of that calamitjq we generously say that we as a Canadian people will do everything to alleviate that distress. Why was it that the people of Saskatchewan were turned down in one case, while the people of Great Britain were supported in the other case? The Canadian people were ready to support a loan to Great Britain, but the fact is that a little extra profit would be made to our exporters who were going to provide the goods. Therefore the representatives of those exporters were entirely in accord with the provisions of that loan.
I voted for that loan, but it was not in order that we might make money out of the misery of the British people or take it from the poeketbooks of the Canadian people. Along with other members, I supported it from a humanitarian point of view. Whenever there is a calamity such as the one which affected the people of Saskatchewan, or the one which affected the people of Great Britain, or the one which affects the soldier settlers at this time, we should search our hearts and not our ledgers in order to find out whether or not the need is worthy of support.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) asked me whether I would support his resolution. I appeal to him to wipe out this debt which has been paid in hardship, in toil and in suffering. If he refuses to do that, then of course I shall still have to support the resolution. I must do that if we are going
Soldier Settlement

to be too hard or too calloused to do the thing that is right. But it is better than nothing and for that reason I will support it. However, I appeal to the minister to withdraw this resolution and replace it with another giving title to those soldier settlers who still have not paid the Canadian people the money that they nominally owe.
